# Weekly newsletter for a Discord community

Read a week of a community's Discord channels and return the members' newsletter in the team's fixed format, as HTML ready for the email tool: the week in a few lines, the new members welcomed, a section for each channel in the server's order with each conversation given as its outcome, and the news of each local hub, in English whatever language a message was written in.

`github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1` · [bundle.mthds](bundle.mthds)

## The sample

[The sample week of a fictional community, in inputs.json](inputs.json)

## What you get

Run on production on 26 September 2026, from the package's files, in 19 seconds. This is what it returned:

<div>
<h3>☀️ Weekly Summary</h3>
<p>We welcomed new members this week. Members shared a completed walnut sideboard, a first café-stool commission, a student’s steam-bent ash chair and progress on a cherry writing desk. The liveliest technical discussion covered clamping a five-board oak top: use clamps every 20–25 cm, alternate them above and below with cauls, and ensure the boards are properly acclimated and closely matched in moisture. Coming up: the monthly video call is next Thursday at 19:00 Paris time, and the Lyon meet-up is on Saturday 10 October at 10am in Villeurbanne.</p><h3>🙌 New members</h3>
<ul><li>Aurélie Brunet is a cabinetmaker making kitchen and dining furniture in a two-person workshop near Nantes, France, mainly in oak and ash. She joined to seek a second opinion on pricing her first large commission on her own before sending the quote.</li><li>Tomasz Wierzbicki is a joiner in Bristol, UK, making staircases and window frames for renovation work and beginning to build small tables in the evenings. He is happy to answer questions about stairs.</li><li>Nadia Haddad teaches adult woodworking classes and builds chairs in Montréal, Quebec, with a focus on steam-bending. She is looking to swap offcuts and for ideas on keeping beginners safe on the bandsaw.</li><li>Olumide Adeyemi is a final-year furniture design student in Lyon, France, on placement at a small workshop until December. He joined to learn about pricing, quoting and finding clients, and plans to share his graduation piece when it is finished.</li></ul><h3>show-your-work</h3><p>Karin Lindqvist finished a walnut sideboard for the couple she mentioned last month, with four doors, a sliding-dovetail carcass and hand-cut finger pulls. It took 61 hours, nine more than quoted, mostly on the doors; in response to Samuel Okafor&#39;s question about the grain match, Karin said she resawn and bookmatched one 60 mm board she had saved for two years.</p><p>Hugo Martel shared his first commission from the market stall: six oak stools for a bakery café. The owner&#39;s requirement that they stack made the leg splay a puzzle.</p><p>Nadia Haddad shared a student&#39;s first chair from her autumn class. Made from ash with a steam-bent back, the student completed every joint herself.</p><p>Priya Raman shared progress on a cherry writing desk, with the drawer boxes glued up. She used hand-cut half-blind dovetails on the fronts and machine-cut joints on the backs.</p><h3>techniques</h3><p>Tomasz Wierzbicki asked how to clamp a 90 cm oak top made from five boards after his last one cupped. Karin Lindqvist, Samuel Okafor and Priya Raman recommended clamps every 20–25 cm, alternating above and below with end cauls; matching board moisture, allowing at least three weeks’ stickered acclimation in autumn, aiming for boards within 1 percent of each other and 8–10 percent for indoor furniture, and alternating growth rings when appearance allows. Tomasz said he had not checked the moisture and had left the boards in the workshop for a week.</p><p>Olumide Adeyemi asked how far to offset the peg hole when drawboring the mortise-and-tenon joints on his graduation bench. Hugo Martel recommended about 1.5 mm in oak for a 10 mm peg, warning that more than 2 mm can split the tenon cheek or snap the peg, and suggested making a test joint from offcuts of the same board.</p><h3>finishing</h3><p>Aurélie Brunet asked why hardwax oil on the underside of a table was still tacky after three days in a 12°C workshop. Karin Lindqvist said cold temperatures below 15°C slow curing and excess oil left on the surface is usually the cause, advising one very thin coat and a firm wipe after 20 minutes; Nadia Haddad suggested shellac for small winter projects, while noting it is unsuitable for dining tables because of water and heat. Aurélie wiped the oil back hard and moved the table into the house, where it was dry by the next morning.</p><h3>tools-and-sharpening</h3><p>Olumide Adeyemi asked about bench-chisel sharpening angles after receiving 25° and 30° advice. Samuel Okafor said a 25° primary bevel with a 30° microbevel suits most work, with steeper angles for chopping hardwood mortises and shallower ones for paring softwood.</p><p>Hugo Martel said that after a month without a honing guide, his edges had become rounder. He is going back to using the guide.</p><p>Tomasz Wierzbicki is giving away eight old 250 mm table saw blades, most still sharp, after switching to a track saw for sheet goods. They are free to anyone in the Bristol hub who can collect.</p><h3>commissions-and-pricing</h3><p>Aurélie Brunet asked whether a €4,800 quote for a solid oak extending dining table, from 180 cm to 240 cm for a family of six, was realistic given €1,150 in timber and hardware and an estimated 70 hours. Karin Lindqvist, Hugo Martel and Priya Raman advised calculating a sustainable hourly rate including overheads and unpaid work, pricing the extension mechanism separately, and setting clear limits on included design revisions; Aurélie recalculated to €5,900 with design included and the mechanism as its own line, and planned to send the quote tomorrow.</p><h3>sawdust-lounge</h3><p>Samuel Okafor found a 1950s hand plane at a car boot sale for 4 pounds; it needs a new iron and a lot of love. Hugo Martel backed Samuel’s view that there is no such thing as enough planes—only not enough wall.</p><p>Priya Raman reminded members that the monthly video call is next Thursday at 19:00 Paris time. The topic is how each person handles a client who changes the design after the timber is cut.</p><h3>🌎 Geographic hubs</h3><h4>🇫🇷-lyon</h4><p>Julien Ferrand announced this month’s meet-up on Saturday 10 October at 10am in his workshop in Villeurbanne, with a sharpening demonstration and coffee. Attendance is limited to 12; Olumide Adeyemi said he will come and can follow the demonstration despite his French still being slow.</p><p>Julien Ferrand said the group oak order has reached 3 m³, and the sawmill will deliver on 21 October. There is still space for about 0.5 m³ for anyone who would like to join.</p><h4>🇬🇧-bristol</h4><p>Tomasz Wierzbicki said that four people are sharing a van to the timber yard on the 17th, with room for one more order if it fits in a 3-metre bed. Samuel Okafor took up the space for a few ash boards for chair legs and offered to bring coffee.</p><h4>🇨🇦-montreal</h4><p>Nadia Haddad announced that her January evening course is full and has opened a waiting list. She asked for ash offcuts longer than 60 cm for bending exercises, and Émile Tremblay will drop off around ten 70 cm offcuts on Thursday.</p>
</div>

**Takes** `discord_channel_updates`, a list of `DiscordChannelUpdate`.

**Returns** a `HtmlNewsletter`: The week's newsletter as HTML, ready to paste into an email tool.

## Try it in your chatbot

With the Pipelex MCP in ChatGPT or Claude ([add it once](https://github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-mcp)), ask:

```text
Run github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1 with the sample inputs in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.1/methods/discord_newsletter/inputs.json
```

In Claude Code or Codex with the [Pipelex plugin](https://github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-plugins), the same sentence runs through `/pipelex-run`.

## Put it in your code

Each call runs the method on the hosted API with your `PIPELEX_API_KEY` ([create one](https://app.pipelex.com)).

The sample inputs are too long to write out here, so each snippet below fetches them from the method's [`inputs.json`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.1/methods/discord_newsletter/inputs.json).

<details>
<summary>TypeScript</summary>

```bash
npm install @pipelex/sdk
```

```ts
import { PipelexApiClient } from "@pipelex/sdk";

const response = await fetch("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.1/methods/discord_newsletter/inputs.json");
const inputs = (await response.json()) as Record<string, unknown>;
const client = new PipelexApiClient({ apiKey: process.env.PIPELEX_API_KEY });
const result = await client.startAndWaitForResult({
  method_ref: "github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1",
  inputs,
});
console.log(result.main_stuff);
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Python</summary>

```bash
pip install pipelex-sdk
```

```python
import asyncio

import httpx
from pipelex_sdk.client import PipelexAPIClient


async def main() -> None:
    inputs = httpx.get("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.1/methods/discord_newsletter/inputs.json").json()
    async with PipelexAPIClient() as client:
        result = await client.start_and_wait(
            method_ref="github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1",
            inputs=inputs,
        )
        print(result.main_stuff)


asyncio.run(main())
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Any HTTP client</summary>

The start call answers at once with the run's id, or with the reason it refused the run; the results call answers 202 while the run is going, 200 with the results once it has completed, and 409 if it failed. The snippet uses `jq` to wrap the sample inputs into the start call's body and to read the id.

```bash
START=$(curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.1/methods/discord_newsletter/inputs.json |
  jq -c '{method_ref: "github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1", inputs: .}' |
  curl -s https://api.pipelex.com/v1/start \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIPELEX_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d @-)
RUN_ID=$(printf '%s' "$START" | jq -r '.pipeline_run_id // empty')
if [ -z "$RUN_ID" ]; then printf '%s\n' "$START"; else
  until [ "$(curl -s -o results.json -w '%{http_code}' https://api.pipelex.com/v1/runs/$RUN_ID/results \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIPELEX_API_KEY")" != 202 ]; do sleep 5; done
  cat results.json
fi
```

</details>

In a project you already have, ask your agent for `/pipelex-integrate github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1`: it generates the result's types and writes one typed call.

## Make it an app

```bash
npm create @pipelex/method-app@latest newsletter-app -- --method github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1
make -C newsletter-app serve
```

The form and the result view come from the method's contract. `make serve` prints the app's URL once the page answers, and `make stop` stops it. Your agent does the same with `/pipelex-scaffold`.

## Make it yours

Ask your agent:

```text
Copy github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1 into ./newsletter, add a Coming up section after the week's summary, listing every event and deadline announced in the channels with its date, prove it on the sample, and save it to my Pipelex account.
```

From then on every door above takes your method's id (`mt_…`) in place of the address, and your chatbot lists it among your methods.

## Run it on your own machine

With the Pipelex runtime and your own provider keys ([set it up](https://docs.pipelex.com/latest/get-started/run-it-yourself/)):

```bash
curl -sLo inputs.json https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.1/methods/discord_newsletter/inputs.json
pipelex run method github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/discord_newsletter@v0.20.1 --inputs inputs.json
```
